prompt: # Role - You are an AI competing in a gaming arena. # Objective - Write a complete Python file that provides the next move for a Othello (Reversi) on an 8x8 board. - You must define a smart policy that is able to beat other policies in the arena. - You will be disqualified if you do not return a legal move string. Therefore, you must always return a legal move string. # Required API The provided python file must implement the following API: ```python def policy(you: np.ndarray, opponent: np.ndarray) -> str: ... ``` # State Representation - You are always the player to move when `policy` is called. - `you` and `opponent` are 8x8 numpy arrays containing only 0/1 integers. - `you[r][c] == 1` means your disc is at row `r`, col `c`. - `opponent[r][c] == 1` means the opponent disc is at row `r`, col `c`. - An empty cell means `you[r][c] == 0` and `opponent[r][c] == 0`. - Positions are valid: never `you[r][c] == opponent[r][c] == 1`. - Move coordinates use algebraic notation: columns `a..h` map to `c = 0..7`, rows `1..8` map to `r = 0..7`. For example, `a4` maps to you[3][0] - The game ends when neither player has a legal move (or the board is full). - Objective: finish with more discs than the opponent; ties are draws. # Action / Return Format - Return a move string like `"d3"` (file letter `a..h` + rank `1..8`). - A legal move must place a disc on an empty cell that flips at least one opponent disc in any direction. - Flips occur along any of the 8 directions where the new disc brackets a contiguous line of opponent discs ending in your disc. - If you have no legal moves, return `"pass"`. You may not return `"pass"` if you have legal moves. # Constraints - You may use any standard Python imports, including numpy. - Your code is allowed 1 second of execution time on a modern 3GHz CPU. # Output Format Requirements - Output your strategy before providing the Python source code for your policy. - Output the Python source code for your policy surrounded by `...` tags. # Example Output The strategy for this policy is... ...
reasoning:
I'm planning to build a strong Othello policy using bitboard-based alpha-beta search with iterative deepening, move ordering, and an evaluation function combining mobility, corners, stability, and positional weights, with exact endgame solving for the final moves. I'll represent the board as 64-bit bitboards and generate moves and flips using shift-based direction loops.

Writing move generation and flip logic...

Finishing the direction table for NW, SE, SW shifts and masks. I'm considering precomputed ray tables per square and direction as a simpler alternative for flip computation, iterating along each ray while opponent discs continue, then checking if it ends on my own disc. For evaluation, I'm planning to combine mobility difference, frontier disc counts for potential mobility, and corner/stability scoring.

Rather than doing a full stability computation each evaluation (too expensive), I'm leaning toward an approximate edge-based stability check anchored at corners, combined with a positional weight table and parity considerations for the endgame.

For the endgame phase, once empties drop to around 10-12, I want to switch to exact disc-differential search with alpha-beta and good move ordering, but I need to be careful about Python's speed limits since a perfect solve at that depth could be too slow without proper time management.

I'll keep this as one iterative-deepening framework where depth-limited search just becomes exact once depth reaches the empty count, using time.perf_counter to enforce a budget around 0.6-0.7 seconds with frequent checks, raising an exception when time runs out so I fall back to the best move from the last completed depth. I'll also add a simple transposition table keyed by board state to store depth, value, and best move for move ordering.

For move ordering, I'm combining transposition table hints with static square weights (corners favored, X-squares avoided) and possibly opponent mobility for deeper nodes, though generating mobility per child is costly. Now I'm setting up the bitboard constants and starting to write the search engine in Python using numpy and bitwise masks for move generation.

Defining move directions...

Writing flip computation logic...

Now I'm designing the evaluation function, weighing disc difference, actual and potential mobility, corner control, and X-square penalties for unstable positions adjacent to empty corners.

For stability I'm adding edge stability from corners and a fast positional weighting scheme grouped by weight value, plus checking Python's popcount options for speed. For stable discs specifically, I'm computing edge stability by extending from owned corners along each edge while the color matches, and treating fully-occupied edges as entirely stable.

I'll skip full iterative stability propagation across all axes since it's too costly, sticking with edge-only stability. I'm also sketching phase-dependent weight tuning — different weights for mobility, potential mobility, stability, corners, and disc count depending on how many discs are on the board (early, middle, late game).

Writing the positional weight table...

I'm thinking through scaling: corner worth about 30 points, X-squares penalized around -12 but only when the adjacent corner is still empty, C-squares similarly conditional, with dynamic adjustments handling whether corners are occupied.

For the search algorithm, I'm sketching a negamax with alpha-beta pruning and transposition table, handling pass moves by flipping sides without decrementing depth, and terminating at depth zero with the static evaluation. The terminal score at game end weights the disc difference heavily to prioritize winning over raw material.

Move ordering will prioritize the transposition table's best move, then static square scores, and at deeper levels factor in resulting opponent mobility despite the extra cost since the pruning gains justify it. At the root, I'm using iterative deepening with a time-based cutoff and reordering moves each iteration based on the previous depth's scores.

For timing, I'll check the clock periodically rather than every node to keep overhead low, targeting roughly 0.65 seconds per move with checks frequent enough to catch overruns before they matter.

I also want to add safety: wrap the search in try/except so any unexpected error falls back to returning a legal move directly from the numpy board, and short-circuit immediately when there's only one legal move available.

Now I'm setting up the bitboard constants and popcount helper, then building ray-direction lookup tables for each square...

Writing move generation with parallel bit-shifting...

Still writing the shift/mask logic...

I'm defining potential mobility as the difference in dilated empty-adjacent squares between opponent and me, favoring more empties bordering opponent discs. Then I'm setting up corner bit masks and starting to work out stable edge configurations for each of the four edges.

Writing evaluation function logic...

Filling out the rest of the positional weight table...

Now I'm setting up the search function with a transposition table, handling the recursive minimax logic with pass detection, timeout checks, and depth-limited evaluation calls.

Adding move ordering with TT best-move preference...

Storing the transposition table entry with the appropriate bound flag based on where the best score fell relative to alpha and beta, then returning. I'm confirming the pass logic terminates correctly and the terminal evaluation just computes disc count difference, and noting the TT should be cleared per top-level call since positions won't recur but memory would otherwise grow unbounded. Now I'm setting up the root-level search function.

Writing search loop code...

I realize the early break on abs(value) >= 1000 is unsafe since terminal scores can appear at shallower depths inconsistently, so I should only stop once depth reaches the empty count, capping depth around 60. I'm also roughly estimating per-node cost from move generation, ordering, and evaluation overhead to gauge how deep I can search within the time budget.

I need to convert the board into a bitboard representation and figure out move notation, plus add error handling that falls back to the static best move if the search fails. Writing the full move generation function...

Adding directional shift logic...

I'm setting up a static square-weight ordering table favoring corners over X-squares, then starting to sketch the root search function with alpha-beta parameters.

For root search, I'm iterating candidate moves, updating alpha as better values are found, tracking the best move, and sorting scored moves for iterative reordering, noting the ordering is only approximate since fail-low bounds distort later comparisons. If a timeout interrupts the root search partway through, I want to fall back to the best move found so far rather than losing progress entirely.

I decide the safest rule is: if the first move of the new iteration completes and its value is set, trust that as the fallback since it inherited the previous best move searched with a full window; any later move that beats it during the same iteration is genuinely better at this depth, so partial results can still update the best move via shared state as the loop runs.

I'll set a time budget of 0.7 seconds and check elapsed time every 256 nodes to keep overhead low. With the overall structure settled, I'm ready to write the code.
